questiontext.text:
Prove that every rational number is the sum of two irrational numbers. Use the method of the example above: a direct proof with a proof by contradiction inside it.

Drag the blocks you need into the box, in order. Not every block is needed: three of the blocks contain a logical mistake. Any order in which each step comes after the steps it relies on is accepted.

[[parsons input="ans1"]] {"steps": {# parsons_encode(proof_steps) #}, "headers": ["Your proof:"], "available_header": ["Drag from here:"]} [[/parsons]]
[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
One correct proof:

Let \(r\) be a rational number. Then \(r = \dfrac{a}{b}\) for some integers \(a\) and \(b\) with \(b \neq 0\).

Then \(r = (r - \sqrt{2}) + \sqrt{2}\).

We know that \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational.

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(r - \sqrt{2}\) is rational. Then \(r - \sqrt{2} = \dfrac{c}{d}\) for some integers \(c\) and \(d\) with \(d \neq 0\).

So \(\sqrt{2} = r - \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{a}{b} - \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ad - bc}{bd}\).

Since \(ad - bc\) and \(bd\) are integers and \(bd \neq 0\), \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational. This is a contradiction, so \(r - \sqrt{2}\) is irrational.

So \(r = (r - \sqrt{2}) + \sqrt{2}\) is the sum of the two irrational numbers \(r - \sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{2}\).

The outer proof is direct and the inner proof is by contradiction, exactly as in the example, with a sum in place of a product. The fact that \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational may come anywhere before the contradiction that uses it, and the inner proof may come before or after the line \(r = (r - \sqrt{2}) + \sqrt{2}\).

The three wrong blocks: assuming that \(r - \sqrt{2}\) is irrational assumes what the inner proof must show; assuming that every rational number is such a sum assumes the whole statement; and two examples prove nothing about every rational number.

questiondescription.text: This question is based on Example 8.9 (pp. 53-54) in Section 9 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

node.description: A valid order of the correct blocks

truefeedback.text: Yes. The outer proof is direct: it writes \(r = (r - \sqrt{2}) + \sqrt{2}\). The inner proof by contradiction shows that \(r - \sqrt{2}\) is irrational, just as the example showed that \(\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{2}}\) is irrational. Unlike the product, this works for \(r = 0\) too.

node.description: Diagnostic: a block with a logical mistake used

truefeedback.text:
[[if test="usedirr"]]

One of your blocks assumes that \(r - \sqrt{2}\) is irrational. To prove by contradiction that \(r - \sqrt{2}\) is irrational, assume the opposite, that it is rational, and show that this is impossible.

[[/if]][[if test="usedall"]]

One of your blocks assumes that every rational number is the sum of two irrational numbers. That is the statement you are proving, so the proof would be circular.

[[/if]][[if test="usedeg"]]

One of your blocks checks two examples and concludes that the statement holds for every rational number. Two cases cannot prove a statement about infinitely many numbers.

[[/if]]
